newsitem.title: CHINA: China quarantine rules improperly used - US official.
newsitem.headline: China quarantine rules improperly used - US official.

text.p: China's use of quarantine rules to bar imports of U.S. wheat and other farm products is improper and is being monitored as China bids to join the world trade community, a senior U.S. trade official said on Tuesday.

"There are very high tariffs and other limitations on agricultural trade, there are phytosanitary standards which we think are improperly used to bar products such as TCK wheat and we will be watching these very carefully," Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told reporters.

Growth in U.S. agricultural exports to China in 1996, at just two percent, was particularly disappointing, he said, adding that part of the reason was China's record grain harvest of 480 million tonnes.

But he singled out Beijing's ban on the import of wheat tainted with a fungus called TCK smut as an example of non-tariff trade barriers that must be dealt with if China wants to become a member of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Washington claims TCK smut is harmless and can be removed from the grain in the milling process with little or no affect on products.

Beijing has banned the import of wheat from the U.S. Pacific northwest for more than 20 years on fears that TCK smut which affects the region's wheat has the potential to cut yields if it finds its way into the domestic Chinese crop.
U.S. wheat growers have said the ban keeps an extra $500 million a year of their wheat out of the China market.
Some scientific experts have said to Reuters TCK smut can cut wheat yields and that Beijing has a legitimate concern.
Beijing and Washington are engaged in ongoing negotiations over this and other quarantine issues.
"With respect to the negotiations, we expect nothing more nor nothing less from China than a commercially viable package," Eizenstat told reporters.

"What we mean by commerically viable is a whole array of areas, from trade rights, to management treatment, transparency, tariff and non-tariff barriers that China has to accept, norms that have been accepted by the WTO," he said.
Eizenstat was in Shanghai for the inauguration of a U.S. commercial centre, Washington's first export promotion office in China and the third in the world after Brazil and Indonesia.
